title: An Apparition to Marius
summary: Hugo describes a hidden house in the Rue Plumet, with a secret passage to the Rue de Babylone, and names its tenant since 1829: Jean Valjean, living there with Cosette and a servant, Toussaint, having left the convent so that Cosette could choose her own life.
details: The chapter opens with the history of a "little house" in the Rue Blomet, now the Rue Plumet, built about the middle of the previous century by a chief justice of the Parliament of Paris to hide a mistress. A pavilion fronts a large overgrown garden; behind it lies a courtyard and a low back building, and from that a walled, roofless corridor winds for a quarter of a league between neighbours' gardens to a second secret door at the far end of the Rue de Babylone. After the Revolution the house stood empty, furnished but unlet, until October 1829, when a man of a certain age quietly took it under the name of M. Fauchelevent, repaired the secret doors, and moved in with a young girl and an elderly maidservant.

The narrator then names them outright: the tenant is Jean Valjean, the girl is Cosette, and the servant is Toussaint, a stammering provincial woman whom Valjean rescued from the hospital. He adds that the reader will have recognised Valjean as promptly as Thénardier did. Nothing drove him from the Petit-Picpus: he left because his happiness there alarmed his conscience. Cosette was being gently steered towards taking the veil, and he decided that to let her renounce the world before she had seen it would be to steal her life for his own comfort. After five hidden years he judged the danger to himself small, and that in any case his own past gave him no right to condemn her to the cloister.

When old Fauchelevent died, Valjean told the prioress he had inherited from his brother, offered the community five thousand francs for Cosette's five years of schooling, and took her away. He carried out himself the small locked valise that smells of embalming, which Cosette teases him about and calls his "inseparable". He also rented two shabby lodgings in distant quarters, in the Rue de l'Ouest and the Rue de l'Homme Armé, where he passes a month or six weeks at a time without Toussaint, so that he can vanish at the first alarm and never again be caught unprepared as on the night he fled Javert.

title: The House with a Secret
summary: How Valjean and Cosette live in the Rue Plumet: she has the pavilion and every comfort, he a bare lodge in the back courtyard; they walk in the Luxembourg, give alms at Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas, and come and go only by the Rue de Babylone door, while he serves in the National Guard as M. Fauchelevent.
details: Cosette and Toussaint occupy the pavilion, with its painted mirrors, gilded boudoir and tapestried drawing-room; Valjean has filled Cosette's room with a canopied bed, a Persian rug, gilt-edged books and a worktable of mother-of-pearl, and keeps the whole house heated all winter. He himself sleeps in a porter's lodge at the end of the back courtyard, with a folding bed, two straw chairs, a few old books, his valise and never a fire. He dines with Cosette and keeps a loaf of black bread for himself. To Toussaint he explained that the young lady is the mistress of the house; he is "a much better thing than the master", the father.

Cosette, taught housekeeping at the convent, runs their modest budget. Every day Valjean takes her for a walk, to the quietest alley of the Luxembourg, and every Sunday to mass at the distant church of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas, where his lavish almsgiving to the poor earned him Thénardier's letter addressed to "the benevolent gentleman" of that church. He takes Cosette to visit the poor and the sick. No stranger enters the house; Valjean fetches water himself from a fountain on the boulevard, and wood and wine are kept in the old grotto by the Rue de Babylone. The letterbox on that door receives only tax notices and summonses to guard duty.

The census of 1831 reached even the convent, so M. Fauchelevent, independent gentleman, belongs to the National Guard and three or four times a year puts on the uniform and mounts guard, glad of a disguise that makes him look like any other taxpayer. He has just turned sixty, the age of exemption, but looks under fifty and claims nothing, since he has no legal existence to claim with. With Cosette he dresses like a retired officer; alone, usually at night, he goes out in a workman's blouse and a cap that hides his face. Toussaint, told by her butcher that he is "a queer fish", answers that he is a saint. The three never use the Rue Plumet gate, which stays locked, and Valjean leaves the garden wild so as not to draw attention. In this, the narrator remarks, he may have made a mistake.

title: Jean Valjean as a National Guard
summary: Hugo describes the Rue Plumet garden, abandoned for half a century and grown into a wild, fragrant thicket behind its rusty gate, and turns it into a meditation on how nothing in nature is small and everything is bound to everything else.
details: Left to itself for more than fifty years, the garden has become extraordinary. Passers-by of forty years ago stopped to peer through the padlocked gate, with its two moss-covered pillars and an undecipherable pediment. Inside there is a stone bench, a couple of mouldering statues, rotting trellises and no paths or lawn, only grass and weeds everywhere. Trees have bent down to the nettles, climbers have climbed, and every growth has mingled with every other so that the enclosure is at once as impenetrable as a forest, as peopled as a city, as fragrant as a bouquet and as solitary as a tomb.

The narrator follows it through the seasons: in spring the thicket drinks the April sap and sheds flowers and dew over the statues, the crumbling steps and even the pavement of the empty street; at midday a thousand white butterflies drift through it like summer snow; at evening honeysuckle and convolvulus pour out their scent while woodpeckers and wagtails settle in the branches. In winter it is black and dripping, and the house shows through. Though the mansions of the Rue de Varennes, the dome of the Invalides and the Chamber of Deputies are a few steps away, the Rue Plumet is a desert, and nature has reclaimed this Parisian corner with the force of a virgin forest.

From the garden Hugo rises to a wider thought: nothing is small. The perfume of the hawthorn may matter to the constellations; a bit of mould is a constellation of flowers and a nebula an anthill of stars; where the telescope ends the microscope begins. All beings and things are bound together in an immense mechanism whose first wheel is the gnat and whose last is the zodiac, and in which the material and the moral worlds flow into one another.

title: Foliis Ac Frondibus
summary: The garden made for a magistrate's gallantries now shelters innocence: Cosette, fourteen when she leaves the convent, plain and half-educated, grows up adoring Jean Valjean, who gives her everything, eats white bread only to stop her eating black, and cannot bring himself to speak her mother's name.
details: The old pleasure-garden has been remade by neglect into a place fit for chaste mysteries, and in it waits a heart ready for love. Cosette left the convent at a little over fourteen, at the awkward age, homely rather than pretty apart from her eyes, timid and bold at once. Her education consisted of religion, devotion, convent "history", geography, grammar, a little music and drawing, and otherwise complete ignorance. Hugo reflects that a girl needs a mother's instinct to be led gently into knowledge of life, and that nothing prepares a girl for passion like the convent, which drives the heart inward. Cosette has had no mother, only many mothers in the plural, and Valjean, all tenderness, knows nothing of such things.

The Rue Plumet, the narrator says, is the sweetest and most dangerous place she could have come to: solitude with a beginning of liberty, a closed garden whose gate opens on the street. Valjean hands the wild garden over to her, and as a child she hunts insects in it while waiting to dream in it. She loves her father with her whole soul; he has gone on reading since his days as M. Madeleine and talks well, and on their walks explains everything to her from his reading and his suffering. She follows him everywhere, preferring his bare lodge and the paved back courtyard to her tapestried drawing-room. When she scolds him for having no carpet or stove he answers that many better men have no roof; when she asks why he eats such horrible bread he says only "Because, my daughter", and when she threatens to eat it too, he switches to white bread.

Of her childhood Cosette keeps only confused memories: two hideous figures, the Thénardiers, as in a dream, and a night journey to fetch water in a forest. She feels she began life in an abyss from which Valjean pulled her. She prays morning and evening for the mother she never knew, and sometimes, leaning her cheek on his white hair, thinks that her mother's soul may have passed into this good man. She does not even know her mother's name. When she asks, Valjean is silent, or smiles, and once the smile ended in a tear. The narrator asks whether prudence, respect, or some fear of handing Fantine's name to another memory seals his lips, and suggests that the dead woman's modesty may itself be keeping her in her grave. When Cosette dreams her mother had wings and must have been a saint, he answers: through martyrdom. And still Valjean is happy, thanking God for being loved by this innocent creature.

title: Change of Gate
summary: Cosette discovers in her mirror, and in Toussaint's remark, that she has become beautiful; within a month she is one of the best-dressed women in Paris, wants to go out, and walks by the railings, while Valjean watches her beauty with dread. Marius sees her again at the Luxembourg after six months.
details: One day Cosette glances at herself and thinks she might almost be pretty. She sleeps badly, decides next morning that she is ugly after all, and for a fortnight does her hair with her back to the glass. Then, in the garden, she overhears Toussaint ask her father whether he has noticed how pretty Cosette is growing. She runs to her mirror, which she has not looked into for three months, and cries out: she has dazzled herself. Her figure has formed, her skin has whitened, her blue eyes have caught fire. She goes back down to the garden feeling like a queen.

Valjean has watched this beauty growing for some time with terror. A man still bleeding from fate, whom the law could seize at any moment, he asks nothing of God or the world except that Cosette should love him; that love heals and crowns him, and anything that might touch it makes him shudder. He does not know what a woman's beauty means, but he senses that it is something terrible, and asks himself what is to become of him. What a mother would have seen with joy, he sees with anguish.

The symptoms follow at once. Remembering a passer-by's remark that she was pretty but badly dressed, Cosette conceives a horror of her merino gown and plush hat and, with a father who refuses her nothing, masters within a month the whole science of bonnets, gowns and mantles. A mother would have told her that a young girl does not wear damask; nobody does. When she first goes out in black damask and a white crape bonnet and asks how he likes her, Valjean answers "Charming!" in a voice like an envious man's, and that evening asks whether she will not put on the old gown again. She laughs at "that disguise". From now on she always wants to go out, prefers the front garden to the back courtyard, and strolls by the railings, while the shy Valjean keeps to his yard like a dog. It is at this point, after a gap of six months, that Marius sees her once more at the Luxembourg.

title: The Rose Perceives That It Is an Engine of War
summary: The story of the Luxembourg is retold from Cosette's side: the exchange of glances that troubled Marius troubled her too, she makes her father stroll towards his bench, and from that day the two adore each other at a distance without a word, she not even knowing the name of what she feels.
details: Cosette, like Marius, was ready to take fire, and Hugo defends the unfashionable truth that people fall in love through a look. She had long since noticed the young man and his fine hair, eyes and voice, though he paid her no attention and so meant nothing to her. On the day their eyes met she went home thoughtfully to the Rue de l'Ouest, where Valjean was spending six weeks, and woke the next morning vexed at the disdainful stranger who now seemed to notice her, and childishly pleased to think she would have her revenge: knowing she was beautiful, she knew she had a weapon.

Marius, as the reader remembers, stayed on his bench and dared not approach. So Cosette went to him, asking her father to stroll in that direction; the first symptom of love in a young man is timidity, in a young girl boldness. That day her glance drove him beside himself and his set her trembling, and from then on they adored each other.

Her first feeling is a deep melancholy, as if her soul had gone dark. She does not know what love is: in the convent even the word amour in songbooks was replaced by tambour or pandour. Not knowing the name of her illness, she loves the more passionately, and the love that has come suits her exactly: an admiration from afar, the deification of a stranger, a vision rather than a lover. She smiles at him with complete frankness, waits impatiently each day for the walk, and tells Valjean in all sincerity what a delicious garden the Luxembourg is. The two never speak, never greet each other, do not know each other's names; they live by gazing at one another.

title: The Battle Begun
summary: Valjean senses Marius, detests him, lays little traps that the young man falls into while Cosette betrays nothing; after Marius follows them to the Rue de l'Ouest and questions the porter, Valjean leaves the Luxembourg for good. Cosette falls silent and pale, and father and daughter suffer side by side without a word.
details: Some instinct warns Valjean of Marius's presence. He sees a young man who now sits far off pretending to read, wears a new coat every day, gloves, perhaps curled hair, and he cordially detests him. Cosette gives nothing away; without knowing what is the matter with her, she knows it must be hidden. Once Valjean cannot help remarking what a pedantic air that young man has, and Cosette answers with perfect calm, "That young man!", as if seeing him for the first time, so that Valjean reproaches himself for pointing him out.

Valjean opens an undeclared war: he changes the hour, changes the bench, forgets his handkerchief, comes alone, and Marius blunders into every snare, while Cosette stays so imperturbable that Valjean concludes the ninny is mad about her and she does not know he exists. Only once does she slip, saying "What, already?" when he rises to leave. Watching Marius, Valjean feels the old wrath of his soul opening again, and rages inwardly at a great booby who comes lounging at the Luxembourg to prowl about his happiness after he has spent sixty years on his knees earning it. He looks at Marius as a dog looks at a thief.

The reader knows the rest: Marius follows Cosette to the Rue de l'Ouest, speaks to the porter, the porter speaks to Valjean, and a week later Valjean has gone, swearing never to set foot in the Luxembourg or the Rue de l'Ouest again. He returns to the Rue Plumet. Cosette asks no questions, afraid of betraying herself, and he, with no experience of these miseries, does not understand her silence. Three months on he offers the Luxembourg; her face lights up, they go, and Marius is not there. The next day she declines, sadly and gently. Valjean sits up whole nights asking what is in Cosette's mind, and looks back with despairing longing to the convent he left of his own free will. Cosette, for her part, languishes, no longer noticing seasons or weather, and shows him nothing but her pallor; each asks the other what is wrong and each answers, nothing.

title: To One Sadness Oppose a Sadness and a Half
summary: On an October dawn at the Barrière du Maine, Valjean and Cosette watch the chain-gang pass on its way to the galleys: seven wagons of collared men beaten, singing and blaspheming in the sunrise. Valjean is petrified; Cosette asks whether they are still men, and days later, pulling a daisy to pieces, asks him what the galleys are like.
details: Valjean, who sometimes becomes childish in his grief, envies a general in full uniform and dreams that gold lace might dazzle Cosette back to him. The two have kept one habit from happier days: walks to see the sunrise in the poor fields near the barriers, where Cosette becomes a little girl again and weaves poppy garlands. One morning in October 1831, at daybreak near the Barrière du Maine, Valjean sits on some planks at a timber-yard gate, sunk in thought, when Cosette says someone is coming.

A noise turns into a convoy of seven wagons. The first six are long ladders on wheels, each drawn by four horses and carrying twenty-four men seated back to back with their legs dangling, an iron collar on every neck and a single chain running behind them all; the seventh is an open rack wagon piled with pots and chains among which sick men lie bound. A double file of ragged guards in three-cornered hats, with sabres, muskets and cudgels, marches alongside, and mounted gendarmes ride at head and rear. The prisoners, livid with cold, in wooden shoes and a harlequin's rags, say nothing while the escort curses and cudgels fall; children run laughing behind. Then the sun rises and the whole mass erupts into grins, oaths and songs, one wagon striking up a popular potpourri, while a crowd of market-gardeners and bourgeois gathers to stare. Dante, the narrator says, would have seen his seven circles on the march.

Valjean's eyes become those of a man seeing a vision; he tries to rise and flee and cannot move. Then he remembers: this is the usual route, the detour taken to spare the King at Fontainebleau the sight, and thirty-five years ago he passed through this barrier himself. Cosette, terrified in another way, asks what those men are. Convicts, he says; going to the galleys. As the cudgelling redoubles she asks whether they are still men. "Sometimes," he answers. The gang, the narrator adds, had left Bicêtre before dawn and would go round by Le Mans, lengthening the journey by days.

Valjean goes home overwhelmed and does not notice Cosette's further questions, but hears her murmur that evening that she would die if she met one of those men close by. Next day there happen to be public festivities, a review in the Champ de Mars and fireworks at the Étoile, and Valjean, putting on his National Guard uniform as if taking shelter, takes her to them and believes the vision has been erased. Some days later, standing in her morning wrapper on the garden steps and pulling a daisy to pieces, Cosette turns her head and asks: "Father, what are the galleys like?"

title: The Chain-Gang
summary: Their life clouds over; only visits to the poor remain, among them the visit to the Jondrette garret. The next day Valjean comes home with a burn on his arm that keeps him in bed a month; Cosette nurses him, the old intimacy returns, spring brightens her, and he blesses the wound and even the Thénardiers.
details: One diversion survives their sadness: carrying bread and clothing to the hungry and cold, visits on which they recover something of their old ease, and Cosette is sometimes merry in the evening afterwards. It was in this period that they went to the Jondrette den. The next morning Valjean appears in the pavilion as calm as ever but with a large inflamed wound like a burn on his left arm, which he explains away. It keeps him indoors with fever for a month, and he refuses a doctor: "Call the dog-doctor," he tells Cosette.

Cosette dresses the wound morning and evening with such happiness at being useful that Valjean's fears dissolve. She deserts the pavilion for his little lodge, spends her days beside him and reads him books of travel; she sings him the melancholy songs she learned from Sister Sainte-Mechtilde at the convent. The Luxembourg, the prowling young stranger and Cosette's coldness all fade, and he tells himself he imagined it all. Even the discovery of the Thénardiers in the Jondrette hovel slides over him: he escaped, his trace is lost, and he thinks of them only to pity a family in such distress, now in prison and harmless. Cosette never mentions the Barrière du Maine again.

When spring comes he urges her to walk in the garden, and to please him she does, usually alone, since he hardly ever goes there himself, probably for fear of being seen through the railings. As March lengthens the days and April arrives, the blackness leaves her spirit without her noticing, and when she coaxes her convalescent father into the sunlight for a quarter of an hour, supporting his arm, she laughs every moment. Valjean whispers again what a good wound it was and feels grateful to the Thénardiers. Once healed, he resumes his solitary twilight walks, and the narrator warns that no one strolls alone through the empty regions of Paris without some adventure.

title: A Wound Without, Healing Within
summary: Hungry Gavroche, about to raid M. Mabeuf's apple-house, hides under the hedge and watches Montparnasse attack an old passer-by who overpowers him, lectures him on the hard labour of idleness and theft, and hands him his purse. Gavroche picks the purse from Montparnasse's pocket and tosses it over the hedge to Mabeuf.
details: Gavroche has eaten nothing for two days. Out beyond the Salpêtrière, in the straggling village of Austerlitz, he remembers a garden with an apple-tree and a badly fastened fruit-house. As he is about to climb the hedge at dusk he hears voices: on a stone bench sits the old man of the garden, and his housekeeper is listing their debts. She calls him Monsieur Mabeuf; he calls her Mother Plutarque, and Gavroche thinks both names a farce. They owe three quarters' rent, the greengrocer will send no more wood, the butcher and baker refuse credit. To each complaint the old man answers mildly: there is the sun; he does not digest meat; there are apples in the apple-room; he has no money. She goes in, and Gavroche, moved, curls up under the hedge behind the bench instead of robbing it, and dozes with one eye open.

Two figures appear in the pale lane: an elderly, plainly dressed bourgeois strolling slowly, and behind him a slim, elegant young man with a rose in his mouth whom Gavroche knows at once as Montparnasse. Gavroche pities the old man but knows the two of them together would be two mouthfuls for such a ruffian. Montparnasse springs; a moment later it is Montparnasse on the ground with a knee on his chest. The old man makes him stand, holds both his arms in one hand, and questions him: nineteen years old, strong, healthy; why not work? It bores him. His trade? An idler. What would he like to be? A thief.

Then, in a gentle voice, the old man delivers a long harangue which Gavroche hears every word of. Idleness, he says, is the most laborious of lives. The idler who will not be a workman becomes a slave: he will tear his sheets into ropes, climb chimneys and sewers, hollow out a sou to hide a watch-spring saw, and his reward will be the dungeon. He will enter at twenty rosy and white-toothed and come out at fifty bent and broken; the hardest of all work is thieving, and it is less disagreeable to be honest. He ends by asking what the young man wanted of him, his purse? Here it is. He puts it in Montparnasse's hand and walks calmly away. The narrator asks who this goodman was and says the reader has surely guessed.

Montparnasse stands amazed, and for the first time in his life thinking. Gavroche creeps up behind him, slips his hand into the back pocket of the fine black coat, lifts the purse, crawls back to the hedge, flings it over onto Father Mabeuf's foot and runs. Mabeuf wakes, opens it, and finds small change in one compartment and six napoleons in the other. Mother Plutarque pronounces that it has fallen from heaven.

title: Mother Plutarque Finds No Difficulty in Explaining a Phenomenon
summary: Cosette's grief fades into near-forgetfulness; she notices a handsome lieutenant of lancers who passes the gate daily, Théodule Gillenormand, and watches for him, at the very moment Marius is sinking towards despair.
details: Four or five months on, nature, spring and youth have healed Cosette's grief without her knowing it. One day she catches herself thinking that she no longer thinks of Marius. That same week a handsome officer of lancers passes the gate: wasp-waisted, blue-eyed, fair, with waxed moustaches, a cigar and a glazed schapka, vain, insolent and good-looking, the reverse of Marius in every way. She supposes he belongs to the regiment barracked in the Rue de Babylone. The next day he passes again and she notes the hour; from then on she sees him nearly every day.

His comrades notice the pretty creature who is always in the untidy garden behind the rococo railings when the lieutenant goes by, and tell him so. The officer, whom the reader already knows, is Théodule Gillenormand, and he replies that he has no time to look at all the girls who look at him. The narrator sets this against Marius at the same moment, descending towards agony and longing only to see her once before he dies; had he seen her gazing at the lancer he would have died of grief. Whose fault? No one's: Marius is a temperament that buries itself in sorrow, Cosette one that plunges in and comes out again.

Hugo adds that Cosette is passing through the dangerous phase in which a girl's lonely heart, like a vine tendril, clings to whatever is nearest, a marble column or a tavern post, and that real misalliance is a misalliance of souls. What does her soul hold? Passion lulled, something limpid at the surface with the officer's image reflected in it, and perhaps a memory lingering at the bottom. Cosette herself does not know. Then a singular incident occurs.

title: Solitude and the Barracks Combined
summary: While Valjean is away on one of his short unexplained journeys, Cosette hears footsteps in the garden at night, and the next evening sees beside her own moonlit shadow the shadow of a man in a round hat. Valjean keeps watch for three nights and then laughs it away as the shadow of a chimney-pot.
details: In the first fortnight of April Valjean goes away for a day or two, as he does from time to time, usually when money runs short; where he goes no one knows, though Cosette once rode with him as far as the Impasse de la Planchette. He says he will be back in three days. That evening Cosette, alone in the drawing-room at ten o'clock, sings the huntsmen's chorus from Weber's Euryanthe at her piano-organ, and afterwards seems to hear a man's soft tread in the garden. From her window upstairs she sees nothing in the full moonlight and puts it down to the music.

The next evening, towards nightfall, she thinks she hears the sound again among the trees and dismisses it as branches rubbing. Coming out of the thicket onto the little lawn, with the moon behind her, she sees her own shadow on the grass and beside it another, clearly outlined, wearing a round hat: the shadow of a man standing a few paces behind her. For a moment she cannot speak or move. When she turns there is no one, and a bold search of the thicket as far as the gate finds nothing. Two hallucinations in two days she cannot believe, and phantoms do not wear round hats.

Valjean returns and she tells him, hoping to be called a little goose. Instead he grows anxious, says it cannot be anything, and goes out to examine the gate closely. That night she wakes, hears someone by the steps, opens her shutter and sees a man in the garden with a big club; the moon shows her it is her father. He spends that night and the next two in the garden. On the third night he calls her to the window, laughing, and shows her on the turf a shadow with a round hat, cast by a hooded sheet-iron chimney-pipe on a neighbouring roof. She laughs with him and her fears vanish. The narrator notes what neither of them asks: whether the chimney really stood in that direction, whether the moon had been in the same place, and why a chimney-pot's shadow should take fright and disappear when someone turns to look at it. A few days later a fresh incident occurs.

title: Cosette's Apprehensions
summary: One April evening Cosette finds a large stone on her bench by the railings that was not there a moment before; she flees indoors in real fear and has Toussaint bar the house. In the morning she lifts the stone and finds an unaddressed envelope holding a little notebook of numbered pages in a fine hand.
details: Near the street railings stands a stone bench screened by yoke-elms but reachable by an arm thrust through the gate. One evening that April, with Valjean out, Cosette sits there after sundown in an objectless twilight sadness; the narrator wonders whether Fantine is in that shadow. She takes a slow turn round the dewy garden, and when she comes back there is a fair-sized stone on the seat she just left. The thought that an arm reached through the railings to put it there frightens her properly this time. She runs into the house and bolts the garden door.

She asks Toussaint whether her father is back (the narrator notes here that Toussaint stammers and asks leave not to transcribe it any further) and whether the garden shutters are barred every night. Toussaint assures her she fastens them up like a prison, then frightens her thoroughly with a speech about lone women, men coming in at night to cut one's throat and blunt knives. Cosette dares not even mention the stone for fear of having the gate opened. She makes Toussaint go over the house from garret to cellar, locks herself in, looks under her bed and sleeps badly, dreaming of a stone as big as a mountain.

At sunrise she laughs at her night terrors, lumps the stone with the footsteps and the round-hatted shadow as things she dreamed, and goes down to the bench; the stone is there, and she breaks into a cold sweat. Daylight turns terror to curiosity. She lifts the stone and finds a white envelope with no address and no seal, containing a small notebook of numbered pages covered in a fine, rather pretty handwriting. There is no name. It must be for her, since a hand left it on her bench; from whom? Trying and failing to look away, she begins to read.

title: Enriched with Commentaries by Toussaint
summary: The chapter is the notebook itself: a sequence of unsigned meditations on love as the reduction of the universe to one being, on parted lovers who correspond through birds and flowers, on a lost address, a smile under a white crape bonnet, and a wish to lie hand in hand in the same grave.
details: The pages are short aphorisms and sighs set down at different times. Love, they say, is to shrink the universe to a single being and expand a single being to God; it is the greeting of angels to stars; to love someone is to make them transparent to God behind everything. Certain thoughts are prayers, and there are moments when the soul is on its knees whatever the body is doing. Parted lovers who cannot write send each other birdsong, the scent of flowers, children's smiles and starlight; spring itself is a letter the writer sends to her.

The writer claims that God can add nothing to lovers' happiness but endless duration, that a woman is a sweeter radiance and a greater mystery than any star, and that when a woman passes emitting light as she walks, one is lost, and nothing remains but to think of her until she is forced to think of you. Love is composed of the infinitely great and the infinitely little, in despair over a lost glove, enchanted by a found handkerchief. Then a fragment of dialogue: does she still come to the Luxembourg? No. Is this the church where she hears mass? She no longer comes. Does she still live in this house? She has moved; she left no address. What a melancholy thing not to know the address of one's soul.

The notebook grows darker: the writer dwells in night since a being went away and carried off his sky; he would be content to lie in the same grave hand in hand, touching a finger now and then. To die of love is to live in it. He describes meeting in the street a very poor young man in love, with holes in his elbows, water in his shoes and stars in his soul, and closes with the thought that if there were no one who loved, the sun would go out. Nothing in the pages is signed, dated or addressed.

title: A Heart Beneath a Stone
summary: Cosette reads the notebook three times and knows at once who wrote it; the lancer, passing at his usual hour, now looks hideous to her. She hides the pages in her bosom, falls back into love, and credits angels with a chance that was in fact a note tossed from one thief to another over the roofs of La Force.
details: As Cosette lifts her eyes from the last page the handsome officer passes the gate at his hour, and she thinks him hideous. The fifteen pages are in one hand but in inks of different blackness, written on different days, without order or plan: a mind unfolding sigh by sigh. Her convent education spoke always of the soul and never of love, as one might speak of the firebrand and never of the flame; these lines reveal to her all at once love, sorrow, destiny and eternity. A letter without name, address, date or signature, a love-letter from a phantom to a shade, written with one foot in the grave and one finger in heaven.

From whom? She does not hesitate for an instant: one man only, him. It was he who wrote, he who thrust his arm through the railings; while she was forgetting him he found her again. But had she forgotten him? Never, she tells herself; the fire was only smothered, and now it blazes through her whole being. She reads the pages a third time, recognising in them what she had already read in his eyes, and when Lieutenant Théodule rattles his spurs past the gate and feels obliged to smile at her, she finds him insipid, foppish, impertinent and extremely ugly, and would gladly throw something at his head.

She shuts herself in her room, learns the manuscript by heart, kisses it and puts it in her bosom. All day she is in a daze, hoping for vague things, feeling the paper's corners against her skin, certain that it comes from him and is for her, and telling herself that an intervention of angels, a celestial chance, has given him back to her. The narrator closes on the real shape of that celestial chance: a pellet of bread tossed by one thief to another, from the Charlemagne courtyard to the Lion's Ditch, over the roofs of La Force.

title: Cosette After the Letter
summary: At dusk, with Valjean out, Cosette goes to the bench and finds Marius standing behind her, bareheaded and pale. He pours out how he searched for her and has been coming at night to her garden; she faints into his arms, they kiss, talk for hours, and only at the end exchange names: Marius, Cosette.
details: That evening Valjean goes out and Cosette, without knowing why, dresses her hair carefully and puts on a gown cut a trifle low. At dusk, while Toussaint is busy in the kitchen on the back yard, she goes down through the low branches to the bench. The stone is still there, and she lays her hand on it as if to thank it. Then she feels someone behind her, turns and rises. It is he: bareheaded, thin and pale, in black clothes the twilight barely shows, with something about him of death and night. He has thrown his hat into the thicket. She retreats until a tree stops her, and would have fallen without it.

In a voice she has never heard, barely above the rustle of the leaves, he begs her pardon for coming: his heart was full and he could not go on living as he was. Has she read what he left on the bench? Does she recognise him at all? He reminds her of the day she looked at him near the Gladiator and the days she passed before him, the 16th of June and the 2nd of July, nearly a year ago; he asked the woman who let the chairs, he knew she lived on the third floor in the Rue de l'Ouest, he followed her, then she vanished. At night he has been coming to look at her windows, walking softly so as not to frighten her; the other evening he was behind her and fled when she turned; once he heard her singing and was happy. Let him come sometimes; he thinks he is dying; he adores her.

"Oh! my mother!" she says, and sinks down as if dying. He catches her and holds her, tottering himself, beside himself with love and yet, the narrator insists, without a trace of passion for the body in his arms. She lays his hand on her heart, where he feels the paper, and stammers: you love me, then? Hush, she breathes, thou knowest it. They fall onto the bench, and their lips meet, a kiss and nothing more. They sit in the cool night without feeling the cold stone or wet grass, their hands clasped, and little by little begin to talk, telling each other everything: their dreams, how they adored each other from afar, their despair at losing each other. In a quarter of an hour each has the other's soul. She never asks how he got into the garden; it seems so simple that he should be there. When they have told each other everything she lays her head on his shoulder and asks his name. Marius, he says; and hers? Cosette.

title: Old People Are Made to Go Out Opportunely
summary: The Thénardiers had two more sons after 1823, whom the mother handed to Magnon to replace her own two boys, dead of croup, so that M. Gillenormand's eighty francs a month would keep flowing. After the Jondrette arrests the police raid Magnon's house; the two little boys, locked out, lose the paper with M. Barge's address and wander the streets.
details: Since 1823, as the Montfermeil inn sank into debt, the Thénardiers had two more children, both boys, making five in all. Madame Thénardier, a mother to her daughters only, detested Gavroche and cursed the two youngest, and got rid of them while they were still small, at a profit. The woman Magnon, who had made old M. Gillenormand support the two children she said were his, lost both boys to the croup epidemic on the same day; with them went eighty francs a month, paid punctually in M. Gillenormand's name by his rent-collector, M. Barge, of the Rue du Roi-de-Sicile. In the freemasonry of evil she found two children of the same age and sex: the little Thénardiers became little Magnons, and Magnon moved to the Rue Clocheperce to break the trail. The registry office noticed nothing. Thénardier demanded ten francs a month for the loan of his sons and received it. M. Gillenormand went on visiting the children every six months and saw no change, Magnon telling him how much they resembled him.

Thénardier used the occasion to become Jondrette, and his daughters and Gavroche hardly had time to learn that they had two small brothers. On the evening she gave them up the Thénardier felt, or seemed to feel, a scruple, which her husband cauterised with the remark that Jean-Jacques Rousseau had done even better, and when she worried about the police he assured her that no one looks closely after children who have not a sou. Magnon, a kind of fashionable woman of the criminal world, shared her lodgings with a gallicised English thief known as Mamselle Miss. The two boys, recommended by the eighty francs, were well fed and dressed and treated almost like little gentlemen, better by their false mother than by their real one. Thénardier even remarked once that the father ought to give them some education.

Then the wholesale arrest in the Jondrette garret spread its catastrophe through the underworld. Shortly after Magnon had passed Éponine the note about the Rue Plumet, the police raided the Rue Clocheperce and seized Magnon, Mamselle Miss and everyone in the house. The two little boys were playing in the back yard and saw nothing; when they tried to go in, the door was locked and the house empty. A cobbler across the street gave them a paper their mother had left, with the address of M. Barge, rent-collector, 8 Rue du Roi-de-Sicile, and told them to go there. The elder led the younger, holding the paper in numb fingers; at the corner a gust of wind tore it away, and as night fell he could not find it. They began to wander the streets.

title: The Malicious Playfulness of the Wind
summary: On a freezing, stormy spring evening of 1832 Gavroche adopts two small lost boys turned out of a barber's shop, buys them bread with his last sou, meets a disguised Montparnasse who tells him Babet has escaped, and bedds them down in his home, the great plaster elephant of the Bastille, inside a rat-proof cage of aviary netting. Before dawn Montparnasse's call summons him out to lend a hand.
details: The spring of 1832, the year the cholera reached Europe, blows harsh north winds and frequent thunderstorms. One such evening Gavroche, in a woman's woollen shawl, stands outside a wig-maker's near the Orme-Saint-Gervais pretending to admire a wax bride while planning to pinch a cake of soap. Two neatly dressed little boys of about seven and five come in weeping to beg and are shoved out by the barber. Gavroche runs after them, learns they do not know where to sleep, and with lordly tenderness tells them to come along. On the way up the Rue Saint-Antoine he insults the barber, a portress and a passer-by, gives his shawl to a shivering beggar-girl, and learns that the boys have a papa and mamma but do not know where they are, and that mamma is a lady who lives with Mamselle Miss. The reader, unlike Gavroche, knows who they are from the previous chapter. He finds a sou in his rags, marches them into a baker's, insists on white bread, and divides it into three, keeping the smallest piece.

At the corner of the Rue des Ballets, within sight of the wicket of La Force, a man in blue spectacles greets him: Montparnasse in disguise. Under a porte-cochère Montparnasse tells him that Babet, moved to the Conciergerie that morning, has escaped by turning left instead of right; Gavroche draws a dagger from the cane Montparnasse carries and asks whether he means to fight the police tonight. Montparnasse says only "Things", and mentions a bourgeois who the other day gave him a sermon and a purse that vanished from his pocket a minute later. Asked where he is putting the infants to bed, Gavroche answers: in the elephant. Montparnasse stuffs quills up his nostrils to change his face, and when a police sergeant passes he warns Gavroche in a coded phrase full of the syllable "dig". Gavroche tells him where to find him: ask for Monsieur Gavroche.

Hugo describes the elephant of the Bastille: a forty-foot model in timber and plaster of a monument Napoleon planned, crumbling and forgotten in the south-west corner of the square beside the boarded-up column of July, black with weather, with grass between its legs, melancholy by day and formidable by night. Gavroche gets the boys through the fence, props a workmen's ladder against a foreleg, and coaxes the elder up to a hole in the belly, then carries the younger up and kicks the ladder away. Inside, by the light of a resin "cellar rat", the children see a skeleton of beams and plaster stalactites, with black spots scurrying in the corners. Gavroche's bed is a straw mat and a warm blanket under a pyramid of poles covered with brass aviary netting weighted down with stones, all of it, he explains, borrowed from the monkeys, the giraffe and the Jardin des Plantes. He tucks the little one in like a mother, corrects the boys' vocabulary (crib, darkmans, nut), promises them summers at the Glacière, the theatre, the Opera claque and a look at the executioner, and puts out the light. The rats swarm onto the netting; the five-year-old learns that the rats ate Gavroche's cat and asks whether they would eat them too, and Gavroche gives him his hand across his brother until all three sleep.

Towards the end of the hour before dawn a man soaked through runs from the Rue Saint-Antoine to the elephant and twice gives a parakeet-like cry. Gavroche answers, slides down the leg, and finds Montparnasse, who says they need him and asks him to lend a hand. The boy asks no questions, and the two set off through the file of market-gardeners' carts towards the Rue Saint-Antoine.

title: In Which Little Gavroche Extracts Profit from Napoleon the Great
summary: That same stormy night Brujon and Gueulemer break out of La Force through a chimney and over the wall; Thénardier drugs his sentry and reaches the top of a ruined wall in the Rue du Roi-de-Sicile but his rope is too short. His accomplices below are about to give up when Montparnasse fetches Gavroche, who climbs a flue, ties the rope and brings down his own father.
details: Babet, Brujon, Gueulemer and Thénardier had planned an escape, with Montparnasse to help from outside; Babet got himself away first, as Montparnasse told Gavroche. Brujon, a month in the punishment cell, came out with a woven rope and a plan, and in the decrepit New Building found Gueulemer and a nail. Roofers were relaying the slates, so ladders and scaffolding linked the courtyards. Thénardier, held in close confinement since the night of 3 February in one of the iron cages of the top storey called the Fine-Air, had somehow obtained a bottle of drugged wine and kept, to spike his bread against the rats, an iron bolt.

On the night Gavroche took in the two children, Brujon and Gueulemer pierce the chimney against which their beds stand, the storm covering the noise, climb the flue, force the grating and reach the roof. They fasten Brujon's rope to the wrenched bars, swing across a six-foot gap eighty feet deep to the outer wall, slide down onto the bathhouse roof and let themselves out into the street in under three-quarters of an hour, breaking their rope and leaving a piece on the chimney. Thénardier, warned no one knows how, sees two shadows pass his dormer and recognises Brujon. At two o'clock a young conscript relieves the old soldier on guard; at four the conscript is found drugged asleep beside an empty cage, with a hole in the ceiling, a hole in the roof, a bed-plank gone and his bayonet missing.

Thénardier has found Brujon's rope too short to descend the outer wall. How he reached the top of the ruined back wall of a demolished house at the corner of the Rue des Ballets and the Rue du Roi-de-Sicile, three storeys above the street, no one has ever explained. There he lies in the rain, flayed and exhausted, as four o'clock strikes and the uproar of a discovered escape breaks out behind him with torches running along the roofs. Four men slip into the fenced recess beneath him to confer. From their slang he knows them: Brujon's barrier argot, Babet's old slang of the Temple, Montparnasse who speaks plain French, and Gueulemer by his shoulders. Brujon and Babet argue that the innkeeper has bungled it and been retaken, and that they should go and drink a bottle; Montparnasse grumbles that one does not desert a friend. Thénardier dare not call out; he drops the end of rope into the enclosure. They look up and see him.

He is too numb to tie a knotted rope to the wall himself, and the old plaster stove-flue running up the ruin is too narrow for a grown man; a brat is needed. Montparnasse runs to the Bastille and returns in eight minutes with Gavroche, who tells the ruffians that a young 'un like him is a man and men like them are babes. He takes off his shoes, is lifted onto the shanty roof, and as he is about to climb sees the face above him in the first light and recognises his father, remarking that it won't hinder. He climbs the flue with the rope in his teeth, straddles the wall and knots the rope to the window crossbar; a moment later Thénardier is in the street, cold and fear forgotten, and his first words are to ask whom they are to eat. Brujon raises the Rue Plumet job: an isolated house, a rotten gate, lone women. Babet says Thénardier's girl Éponine looked into it and sent Magnon word there was nothing to be made there; Thénardier says the girl is no fool but it must be seen to. Nobody looks at Gavroche, who waits on a fence-post for his father to turn towards him, then puts his shoes on and goes off to get his brats out of bed. Babet asks Thénardier whether he took a good look at the boy who carried him the rope; it struck him it was his son. "Bah!" says Thénardier. "Do you think so?"

title: The Vicissitudes of Flight
summary: Hugo opens a digression on argot, defending his use of thieves' slang in fiction: every trade has its jargon, but true slang is the language of wretchedness itself, and the historian of a society's depths has as grave a duty as the historian of its battles and kings.
details: The book begins with a Latin word, pigritia, idleness, which Hugo makes the mother of a son, theft, and a daughter, hunger, and of a whole world and dialect, slang. He recalls the outcry when, thirty-four years earlier, he put a thief talking argot into an earlier work, and the same objections raised since against Balzac and Eugène Sue. Slang is horrible, he agrees; but when has horror excluded study? A naturalist does not refuse to examine the viper, nor a surgeon the ulcer. Argot is both a literary phenomenon and a social fact, and properly speaking it is the language of misery.

He anticipates the objection that everyone speaks slang: merchants, stockbrokers, gamblers, soldiers, printers, phrenologists, duchesses, diplomats with their ciphers, classical academicians who call the sea Neptune, and sailors with the heroic slang of the sea. He grants it and sets it aside, reserving the word for the crafty, venomous tongue of combat invented by the last misery when it decides to make war on the whole order of fortunate facts and reigning rights. Preserving even a fragment of such a language, as Plautus preserved Phoenician and Molière the Levantine dialects, is a service to civilisation, and the tongue spoken for four centuries by every form of human misery deserves study more than any provincial dialect.

The historian of manners and ideas, he argues, has a mission no less austere than the historian of events: one records crowns, battles and revolutions in daylight, the other the toiling, suffering, oppressed life underground, descending as brother and judge among those who bleed and those who strike. The two histories interpenetrate; man is an ellipse with two foci, facts and ideas. Slang is the dressing-room where language disguises itself in word-masks and metaphor-rags to perform evil; overheard at the portals of society it sounds like hydras talking. He closes by asking for compassion on the chastised, reflecting that the earth itself resembles a jail and that no one is truly fortunate; the real division is between the luminous and the shady, and the remedy is education, though even those who learn to know and love will still suffer.

title: Origin
summary: Hugo digs into slang as a philologist and geologist: its borrowings from Spanish, Italian, English, German, Latin, Basque and Celtic, its three natural roots in direct word-creation, metaphor and deformation, its constant mutation, and the lessons buried in its metaphors, down to the Châtelet cellar where the galley songs were born.
details: Slang is the tongue of those who sit in darkness; every syllable seems branded. Yet it has its syntax and poetry and belongs in literature: Villon spoke it, and the famous line about the snows of yesteryear uses a slang word, antan. Studied as a geologist studies strata, it is an alluvial deposit in which lie old popular French, Provençal, Spanish, Italian, the Levantine of the ports, English, German, Latin, Basque and Celtic, each accursed race having dropped its layer. Hugo gives examples in each language, from boffete and gat to bichot (from bishop), caleur (from Kellner), cadene (from catena) and the Celtic guedouze for death.

Beyond borrowing, slang has roots in the mind itself. First, direct creation: barbarous, solitary words with no etymology, like taule for the executioner or rabouin for the devil, which both mask and reveal. Second, metaphor, the refuge of the thief plotting a stroke and the prisoner planning an escape: to unscrew the nut is to wring a neck, it lansquines means it rains like a hedge of lancers' pikes. Third, expedient: deforming ordinary words and tacking on terminations in aille, orgue, iergue or uche to throw listeners off. Because it is the dialect of corruption and always seeking concealment, slang decomposes and recomposes faster than any language, so that Cartouche's talk would have been Hebrew to Lacenaire; the Temple preserved the seventeenth-century slang, Bicêtre the slang of Thunes.

Every metaphor holds a lesson. For these men night is la sorgue and man l'orgue, man a derivative of night; a prisoner is a sick man and a condemned man a dead one; the saw that cuts his fetters is a dance-hall, because his first thought on being free is to dance; the head that plots is the Sorbonne and the head that pays la tronche; prison is the college. Hugo then describes the cellar of the Grand-Châtelet, eight feet below the Seine, where men bound for Toulon were chained by the neck to a beam too short to let them lie down, standing in mud for months, and where nearly all the galley songs were born, because song lingers where hope has gone. To inform is "to eat the bit"; a slap is a camoufle, from which Voltaire's camouflet. Slang is language turned convict, and the chapter ends asking whether no deliverer will ever come to the human soul chained like Andromeda in that darkness.

title: Roots
summary: Hugo traces the mood of slang through its songs: for centuries humble and lamenting, in the eighteenth century suddenly insolent and gay, a sign that the lowest classes were losing their sense of guilt and that doctrines were feeding theft. He argues the French Revolution forestalled the jacquerie this portended and made such an uprising impossible since.
details: The old slang of the Court of Miracles, like the cards its vagrants painted with hares roasting a huntsman, breathed a powerless, dejected sadness; its songs were humble enough to draw tears, the thief always the hare in hiding who lies flat and begs, conscious of his guilt. Towards the middle of the eighteenth century the tone changed: prison songs became strident and jovial, sung in a cellar or a wood while a throat was being cut; the rabble began to mock the grand meg and the grand dab and call the King of France the Marquis de Pantin. Hugo reads this gaiety as a grave symptom: the darkened classes were losing the sense of their criminality and feeling some unspoken support among thinkers, as theft began to filter into doctrines and sophisms.

He is careful whom he accuses: not the eighteenth century or philosophy, whose encyclopaedists, physiocrats, philosophers and utopians, Diderot, Turgot, Voltaire and Rousseau, were four sacred vanguards of humanity. Beside them grew sophists, forgotten writers licensed by the King, chief among them Restif de la Bretonne, whose disorganising works were devoured by the unfortunate. In Germany, summed up by Schiller's Robbers, theft rose up against property and labour dressed as theory. When suffering breeds wrath and the prosperous sleep, the result is the jacquerie, the revolt of discomfort against comfort, an earthquake of the people beside which political agitation is child's play.

This peril, imminent at the end of the eighteenth century, the French Revolution cut short: the idea armed with a sword, it closed the door of evil and opened the door of good, ended torture, and gave man a second soul, the right. Hence, Hugo insists, the social catastrophe is now impossible; revolution is the vaccine against jacquerie. Since 1789 the whole people has grown into a sublime individual: he who is free is scrupulous, he who votes reigns, and on days of deliverance there is no longer any populace. His proof is 1848, when the ragpickers of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, barefoot, guarded the wagons carrying the crown jewels of France. The red spectre, he concludes, no longer frightens anyone.

title: Slang Which Weeps and Slang Which Laughs
summary: Closing the digression, Hugo warns that though the jacquerie is gone, society can die of a slow disease, misery; he sets out the duties of foresight, education and labour as a right, affirms his faith that progress will raise the lowest layers out of distress, and admits the hours when the ideal looks like a small star among black clouds.
details: Society need no longer fear the apoplexy of a jacquerie, but it may die of consumption, and social consumption is called misery. The first fraternal obligation and the first political necessity is to think first of the disinherited: to air, enlighten and love them, to lavish education on them, to offer the example of labour and never of idleness, to limit poverty without limiting wealth, to open workshops for every arm, schools for every aptitude and laboratories for every intelligence, and to proportion enjoyment to effort. And all this is only the beginning: labour cannot be a law without being a right. If nature calls itself Providence, society should call itself foresight; a soul starving for light is more heartbreaking than a body starving for bread.

Progress, Hugo affirms, tends towards solution; as humanity rises, the deep layers will emerge naturally from the zone of distress and misery will be abolished by a simple raising of the level. The past is strong at this moment, walking like a conquering corpse with superstition, despotism and ignorance for its legions, but ideas do not flow backwards any more than rivers, and those who say no to the future condemn only themselves. The people sketched by the eighteenth century will be finished by the nineteenth; a force compounded of earth and heaven governs human affairs and conducts them towards equity.

Social philosophy is science and peace, dissolving wrath by studying antagonisms. Civilisations have foundered before, Babylon, Nineveh, Thebes, Rome, for reasons no one knows; but ours lies in the light where its faults can be probed and the remedy found, and it will be saved. Hugo calls these pages an austere interlude in a mournful drama and wishes to end on encouragement, yet confesses that those who follow the social clinics sometimes shake their heads: between the swollen selfishness of the prosperous and the covetous misery of the wretched, the ideal can look like a lost point of light surrounded by monstrous black menaces, though no more in danger than a star in the maw of the clouds.
